learn.hook: A dosa stall with 1 tawa and 2 cooks makes 60 dosas an hour; add a third cook and maybe 80. The production function is the recipe linking inputs to the maximum output.
points: A production function shows the maximum output a firm can produce from given quantities of inputs, with a given technology: q = f(L, K), where L is labour and K is capital.
It is a technical relationship; improved technology changes the function itself.
An output table shows the output for different combinations of L and K; read across a row (K fixed) to see the effect of more labour.
Isoquant (in the NCERT book; check your syllabus): a curve showing all combinations of L and K that give the same output. Isoquants slope downward, and a higher isoquant means a higher output.

example.q: An output table: with K = 2, output is 10, 24, 36 for L = 1, 2, 3; with K = 3, output is 14, 30, 45 for L = 1, 2, 3. What is the output with L = 2, K = 3? What happens if K rises from 2 to 3 with L = 2?
steps: Read row K = 3, column L = 2: output = 30.
With L = 2, output rises from 24 (K = 2) to 30 (K = 3).
example.answer: Output = 30; it rises by 6 units when K rises from 2 to 3.

learn.reallife: A textile mill in Surat can make the same 1,000 metres of cloth with many workers and old looms or with fewer workers and modern looms: two points on the same isoquant.

teach.ask: Gappu's nest workshop uses 3 birds and 2 twig-cutters to build 12 nests a day. 'What's the rule linking inputs and nests called?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The production function gives the maximum output from inputs like labour and capital, for a given technology!
teach.nudge: Good! Is it any output or the maximum output? And what is held fixed?

topics.title: Short run, long run, and TP, AP and MP

learn.hook: A café can hire an extra waiter tomorrow, but building a bigger kitchen takes a year. That difference is the short run versus the long run.
points: Short run: at least one factor (e.g. capital, the building) is fixed; output changes only by varying the variable factor (e.g. labour). Long run: all factors can be varied.
These periods are defined by the flexibility of inputs, not by calendar time; the long run of a tea stall may be weeks, of a steel plant years.
Total product (TP): total output as one variable input (L) changes, other inputs fixed. Average product AP = TP / L.
Marginal product MP = ΔTP / ΔL, or with unit changes MP_L = TP_L − TP_(L−1).
TP is the sum of the MPs; AP at L units is the average of the MPs up to L.

example.q: TP for L = 1, 2, 3, 4: 10, 24, 36, 44. Find AP and MP.

learn.reallife: During festive rush, a sweet shop adds helpers (variable factor) in the same kitchen (fixed factor): a short-run decision.

items.q: TP rises 40 → 52 as L rises 4 → 6. MP?

teach.nudge: Good! How do we get the extra output from the 3rd bird? And output per bird?

topics.title: Numericals on TP, AP and MP

learn.hook: Board papers love this: give any one of TP, AP or MP, and ask for the other two. Master the three links and these become free marks.
points: From TP: AP = TP/L; MP = TP_L − TP_(L−1).
From AP: TP = AP × L; then MP = TP_L − TP_(L−1).
From MP: TP = running sum of MPs; then AP = TP/L.
Always build the TP column first if it is missing; everything else follows.

example.q: AP for L = 1, 2, 3, 4 is 20, 18, 16, 14. Find TP and MP.

learn.reallife: A garment unit manager uses these calculations to decide whether one more tailor on the shop floor adds enough shirts to justify the wage.

teach.ask: Gappu knows his team's AP: 10 nests with 1 bird, 9 with 2, 8 with 3. 'Can I find TP and MP from this?'
teach.praise: Tweet! TP = 10, 18, 24 by multiplying AP by birds; MP = 10, 8, 6 by subtracting!
teach.nudge: Good! How do we get TP from AP first? Then how do we find MP?

topics.title: Law of variable proportions (returns to a factor)

learn.hook: Add workers to one small farm: first they help each other, then they get in each other's way, and finally they trample the crop. Output tells this whole story.
points: Law of variable proportions: when more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor, the MP of the variable factor first rises, then falls, and may eventually become negative.
Phase I, increasing returns to a factor: MP rises, because the fixed factor is better utilised and workers can specialise.
Phase II, diminishing returns to a factor: MP falls but stays positive, because the fixed factor becomes relatively scarce (factor proportions worsen).
Phase III, negative returns: MP becomes negative and TP falls, because too many variable units crowd the fixed factor.
A rational producer operates in Phase II.

example.q: MP of labour on a farm for L = 1 to 7: 10, 14, 12, 8, 4, 0, −3. Identify the phases.
steps: MP falls from 12 down to 0 (L = 3 to 6) without becoming negative: diminishing returns (TP is at its maximum when MP = 0)
example.answer: Phase I: L 1–2; Phase II: L 3–6; Phase III: L 7

learn.reallife: In parts of rural India, many family members work on one small plot; the extra worker adds little or nothing to output, a sign of diminishing or even zero marginal product.

Reason (R): In that stage, extra units of the variable factor reduce total output.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false

quiz.explain: A few workers cannot use a big fixed input fully; more workers use it better.

teach.ask: Gappu keeps adding birds to one tree to build nests. 'First output shoots up, then slows, then falls! Why?'
teach.praise: Tweet! MP rises, then diminishes as the tree gets crowded, then turns negative. That's the law of variable proportions!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to MP as more birds crowd the same tree? Name the three phases.

topics.title: Shapes of TP, MP and AP curves

learn.hook: Three curves, one story. When you draw TP, AP and MP together, their key points line up exactly. Examiners check those alignments.
points: TP first rises at an increasing rate (MP rising), then at a diminishing rate (MP falling but positive), reaches its maximum when MP = 0, and falls when MP is negative.
MP and AP curves are both inverse-U shaped: they rise, reach a maximum and then fall.
MP cuts AP at the maximum point of AP.
When MP > AP, AP rises; when MP = AP, AP is at its maximum; when MP < AP, AP falls.
AP stays positive as long as TP is positive, but MP can become negative.

example.q: TP for L = 1 to 6: 10, 24, 36, 44, 48, 48. Where is AP maximum, and where is TP maximum?
steps: TP maximum (48) where MP = 0, at L = 6
example.answer: AP max = 12 (where MP = AP); TP max = 48 (where MP = 0)

learn.reallife: Factory managers who track output per worker (AP) and extra output of the last worker hired (MP) can see that hiring beyond the point where MP falls below AP lowers average productivity.

topics.title: Returns to scale and long-run costs

learn.hook: Double every input of a pizza chain, ovens, chefs, outlets, and does output exactly double? That's the long-run question of returns to scale.
points: Note: returns to scale and long-run costs are in the NCERT book; check whether your school examines them this year.

Returns to scale describe what happens to output when ALL inputs increase in the same proportion: constant (output rises in the same proportion), increasing (more than proportionately) or decreasing (less than proportionately).
Cobb–Douglas production function: q = x1^a × x2^b. Returns to scale are constant if a + b = 1, increasing if a + b > 1, decreasing if a + b < 1.

In the long run all inputs are variable, so there are no fixed costs. The long-run average cost (LRAC) curve is U-shaped: it falls under increasing returns to scale, is flat under constant returns, and rises under decreasing returns.
The long-run marginal cost (LRMC) curve cuts LRAC at LRAC's minimum point.

example.q: q = x1^0.5 × x2^0.5. Find output when x1 = 4, x2 = 9, and identify the returns to scale.
steps: a + b = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 → constant returns to scale
Check: doubling inputs to (8, 18) gives √8 × √18 = √144 = 12, exactly double.

learn.reallife: Large Indian car plants enjoy increasing returns to scale up to a point, which is why carmakers prefer big plants over many small ones.

topics.title: Cost concepts: fixed, variable, average and marginal

learn.hook: A food truck pays ₹500 a day for parking whether it sells 0 or 300 rolls. The cost of ingredients rises with every roll. Two very different kinds of cost.
points: The cost function shows the least cost of producing each level of output, given input prices.

Total fixed cost (TFC): costs that do not change with output (rent, salaries of permanent staff, interest). Total variable cost (TVC): costs that vary with output (raw materials, wages of casual workers). TC = TFC + TVC.
AFC = TFC / q; AVC = TVC / q; AC (SAC) = TC / q = AFC + AVC.
Marginal cost (SMC) = ΔTC / Δq = ΔTVC / Δq (fixed cost does not change). With unit steps, MC_q = TC_q − TC_(q−1).
TVC = sum of MCs up to that output (TFC is not included).

example.q: TFC = ₹100. TVC at q = 1, 2, 3: ₹40, ₹70, ₹90. Find TC, AFC, AVC, AC and MC at q = 3.

learn.reallife: For Indian Railways, track maintenance is largely a fixed cost, while fuel for each additional train is a variable cost.

teach.ask: Gappu's nest factory pays ₹50 rent every day and ₹10 of twigs per nest. 'Which costs are fixed and which are variable? What's my average cost for 5 nests?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Rent is fixed, twigs are variable; TC for 5 nests = 50 + 50 = 100, so AC = ₹20 per nest!
teach.nudge: Good! Which cost stays the same when output changes? How do you find the cost per nest?

learn.hook: Picture cost curves on a graph: one flat line, two rising ones running parallel, a curve that keeps falling, and three U-shapes. Each shape has a reason.
points: TFC is a horizontal straight line. TVC starts from the origin and rises; TC starts from the level of TFC and rises parallel to TVC (the vertical gap is always TFC).
AFC is a rectangular hyperbola: it falls continuously as output rises (AFC × q = TFC is constant) but never touches the x-axis.
SMC, AVC and SAC are U-shaped, because of the law of variable proportions: returns to the variable factor first increase (costs fall), then diminish (costs rise).
SMC cuts AVC and SAC from below at their minimum points. The minimum of SAC lies to the right of the minimum of AVC.
The vertical gap between SAC and AVC equals AFC; it narrows as output rises because AFC keeps falling.

example.q: TFC = 100. At q = 4, AVC = 30 and at q = 5, AVC = 34. Find AFC and SAC at both outputs and the gap between SAC and AVC.
steps: The gap (AFC) narrows as output rises.
example.answer: Gap = AFC: 25 at q = 4, 20 at q = 5

learn.reallife: A newspaper's printing press is a big fixed cost; as circulation grows, the fixed cost per copy (AFC) keeps shrinking, which is why bigger print runs make each copy cheaper.

quiz.q: The AFC curve is a:
quiz.explain: AFC × q = TFC, a constant.
quiz.mistake: Thinks AFC is U-shaped like the other averages

quiz.q: SMC cuts the AVC curve at:
quiz.explain: AVC falls while SMC < AVC and rises when SMC > AVC, so they meet at AVC's minimum.
quiz.mistake: Confuses with product curves, where MP cuts AP at its maximum

quiz.q: TFC = ₹120. What is the vertical gap between SAC and AVC at q = 8?
quiz.mistake: Gives TFC instead of AFC

quiz.q: Why are SAC, AVC and SMC curves U-shaped in the short run?
options: Because of the law of variable proportions
quiz.explain: Increasing then diminishing returns to the variable factor make costs fall, then rise.
quiz.mistake: Uses the long-run reason (returns to scale)

quiz.q: Why does the gap between SAC and AVC narrow as output rises?
quiz.explain: The gap is AFC, which falls as fixed cost is spread over more units.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the gap is MC

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The minimum point of SAC lies to the right of the minimum point of AVC.
Reason (R): After AVC starts rising, SAC continues to fall for a while because the fall in AFC outweighs the rise in AVC.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Falling AFC keeps pulling SAC down a little beyond AVC's minimum.
quiz.mistake: Thinks both minima occur at the same output

quiz.q: TFC = ₹100. At what output is AFC equal to ₹4?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies TFC by AFC

teach.ask: Gappu drew all his cost curves and AFC touched the x-axis. 'Is that right? And why are AC and MC U-shaped?'
teach.praise: Tweet! AFC keeps falling but never touches the axis, AC and MC are U-shaped due to variable proportions, and MC cuts AC at its minimum!
teach.nudge: Hmm, can AFC ever be zero if fixed cost is positive? And why do AC and MC first fall and then rise?

learn.hook: Given a few numbers, an examiner expects you to fill an entire cost table. One golden rule: always find TC (or TVC) first.
points: From TC: TFC = TC at zero output; TVC = TC − TFC; MC = TC_q − TC_(q−1); AFC, AVC and AC by dividing by q.
From MC and TFC: TVC = running sum of MCs; TC = TFC + TVC; then the averages.
From AC: TC = AC × q; then the rest.
Check your table: MC should cut AVC and AC near their minimum values, and AC − AVC should equal AFC.

example.q: TC at q = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4: 100, 140, 170, 190, 220. Find TFC, TVC, MC and AVC.

learn.reallife: Small business owners in Indian MSME clusters use such tables to find the output where cost per unit is lowest.

games.title: From TC to every cost
items: Read TFC as TC at zero output
Find TVC = TC − TFC
Find MC as the change in TC
Divide TFC, TVC and TC by q for AFC, AVC and AC

quiz.q: TC at zero output is ₹150. What is TFC?
quiz.explain: At zero output there is no variable cost, so TC = TFC.
quiz.mistake: Thinks TC at zero output must be zero

quiz.q: TC: q = 0 → 100, q = 1 → 140, q = 2 → 170. What is AVC at q = 2?
quiz.mistake: Uses TC instead of TVC

quiz.q: TC: q = 2 → 170, q = 3 → 190. What is MC of the 3rd unit?
quiz.mistake: Computes AC (190/3) instead of the change in TC

quiz.q: TFC = ₹60; MC of units 1 to 4 is ₹20, ₹15, ₹15, ₹30. What is AC at q = 4?
quiz.mistake: Forgets TFC or divides TVC only

quiz.q: AC at q = 6 is ₹40 and TFC is ₹60. What is AVC at q = 6?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts TFC directly from AC

quiz.q: AC at q = 4 is ₹55 and at q = 5 is ₹54. What is MC of the 5th unit?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the averages

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): TVC can be found by adding up the marginal costs.
Reason (R): Each MC is the addition to variable cost from one more unit.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Summing the increments in variable cost gives total variable cost.
quiz.mistake: Adds TFC into the sum of MCs

quiz.q: TC at q = 0, 1, 2, 3 is ₹50, ₹80, ₹100, ₹130. At which output is AVC lowest?
quiz.mistake: Picks the output with lowest MC instead

teach.ask: Gappu has TC for 0 to 3 nests: ₹60, ₹90, ₹110, ₹140. 'Fill my whole cost table, please!'
teach.praise: Tweet! TFC 60, TVC 0, 30, 50, 80, MC 30, 20, 30, then divide by output for the averages!
teach.nudge: Good! What is TFC here? Remember TC at zero output. Then how do you get TVC and MC?

learn.hook: A street vendor sells pens at a fixed ₹10 each. Every extra pen brings exactly ₹10 more. That simple fact gives three straight-line revenue curves.
points: Total revenue TR = price × quantity = p × q.
Average revenue AR = TR / q = p. AR is always equal to price.
Marginal revenue MR = ΔTR / Δq = change in TR from selling one more unit.
When price is constant (as for a price-taking firm), AR = MR = price at every output, and the AR/MR line is horizontal.
With a constant price, TR is a straight line from the origin with slope equal to the price.

example.q: Price = ₹10. Complete TR, AR and MR for q = 1 to 4.
example.answer: AR = MR = ₹10 throughout; TR rises by ₹10 per unit.

learn.reallife: A farmer selling wheat at the government's fixed procurement price earns the same price on every quintal: AR = MR = price.

games.title: Revenue facts
items: AR is always equal to price.
AR = TR/q = pq/q = p.
With a constant price, MR equals AR.
Each extra unit adds exactly the price.
With a constant price, TR is a straight line from the origin.
TR = p × q with constant slope p.
MR is total revenue divided by quantity.
That is AR; MR is the change in TR.
With a constant price, the AR curve slopes downward.
It is horizontal at the price.

quiz.q: Average revenue is always equal to:
quiz.explain: AR = TR/q = p.
quiz.mistake: Confuses AR with MR in general

quiz.q: A firm sells 25 units at ₹8 each. What is its TR?
quiz.mistake: Adds price and quantity

quiz.q: TR at q = 4 is ₹60 and at q = 5 is ₹75. What is MR of the 5th unit?
quiz.mistake: Gives TR or AR instead

quiz.q: TR = ₹300 at q = 20. What is the price?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies TR by q

quiz.q: When price is constant at all levels of output:
quiz.explain: Each extra unit adds exactly the constant price.
quiz.mistake: Thinks MR always falls

quiz.q: With a constant price, the TR curve is:
options: A straight line through the origin
quiz.explain: TR = p × q rises proportionally with q.
quiz.mistake: Confuses TR with AR

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For a firm selling at a constant price, AR and MR curves are the same horizontal line.
Reason (R): Each additional unit sold adds an amount equal to the price to TR.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Constant MR equal to price means AR = MR = p, a horizontal line.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect constant price with MR

quiz.q: Price is ₹12 per unit. TR at q = 9 minus TR at q = 8 equals:
quiz.explain: 108 − 96 = 12, which is the MR and equals the price.
quiz.mistake: Gives TR at q = 9

teach.ask: Gappu sells nests at ₹20 each. 'What are my TR, AR and MR if I sell 6 nests?'
teach.praise: Tweet! TR = 20 × 6 = ₹120, and with a fixed price AR = MR = ₹20!
teach.nudge: Good! TR is price times quantity. What is the revenue per nest, and the extra revenue from one more nest?
